Front: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier: what does each do, and what is its method?
Back: Predicate<T>: test(T) → boolean, checks a condition. Function<T,R>: apply(T) → R, transforms a value. Consumer<T>: accept(T) → void, performs an action. Supplier<T>: get() → T, produces a value from no input.
Use the default methods and(), or() and negate(), plus the static Predicate.not(). Example: `isValid.and(isHighValue)` returns a new Predicate; the originals are unchanged.

Front: When should you use a custom functional interface like PaymentStrategy instead of Function<Payment, PaymentStatus>?
Back: Both have the same shape, so either works. Use the standard java.util.function types for generic behavior. Use a custom interface for an important domain concept: `strategy.pay(payment)` says more than `function.apply(payment)`, and it gives Spring a clear bean type.

Front: @Qualifier vs List<T> vs Map<String,T> injection in Spring?
Back: @Qualifier gives you ONE specific bean. List<T> gives you ALL beans of type T (good for validators, handlers and pipelines that run every bean). Map<String,T> gives you ALL beans keyed by bean name (good for picking one bean at runtime). If order matters in a List, use @Order or Ordered, not registration order.

Front: A strategy registry does `strategies.get(name)`. What can go wrong, and how do you handle it?
Back: Map.get returns null for an unknown or misspelled bean name, which turns into a NullPointerException later. Check right away and fail clearly, e.g. throw IllegalArgumentException("Strategy not found: " + name). The string keys also tie domain logic to bean names; an enum-keyed map or a supports(method) check removes that coupling.
